variants.title: Choose the family
variants.context: Encoder-only models read both directions and fit classification, extraction, ranking, and embeddings. Decoder-only models attend left to right and fit open-ended generation and tool use. Encoder-decoder models add cross-attention from generated tokens to encoded input and fit translation.
variants.prompt: You need a sentence embedding for ranking and a label for classification, with no generation. Which family?
optionFeedback: A decoder is built to generate.
Two stacks are unnecessary without generation.
variants.hint: Is the output a label, a score, or generated text?
variants.explanation: Choose encoder-only when the output is a bounded label, score, span, or representation.

variants.prompt: One interface must handle open-ended generation and in-context task specification. Which family?

variants.hint: Which family predicts the next token?
variants.explanation: Decoder-only models attend to themselves and earlier positions.

variants.prompt: Translation needs source understanding and target generation with explicit cross-attention. Which family, and what settles the choice?
options: Decoder-only, because one stack always translates better.
Whichever family has the most parameters at the same cost.
Encoder-decoder, settled by measurement on the real workload.
optionFeedback: Decoder-only can translate, but the choice is empirical rather than automatic.
Parameter count is not a quality guarantee, and it says nothing about throughput or tokenizer fit.
Architecture names do not settle the decision; measurements do.

variants.title: Compute attention
variants.context: Scaled dot-product attention: project Q, K, V; take query-key dot products; divide by the square root of the key dimension; replace disallowed scores with a negative-infinite mask; normalize with softmax; take the weighted sum of values.
variants.prompt: Compute one head of scaled dot-product attention. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Replace disallowed scores with an effectively negative-infinite mask value.
Divide by the square root of the key dimension.
Take query-key dot products to get compatibility scores.
Normalize the permitted scores with softmax so they sum to one.
Project the representations into query, key, and value vectors.
Compute the weighted sum of value vectors.

variants.hint: Masking happens before softmax so masked positions get zero probability.
variants.explanation: softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k + mask) V. Test that permitted weights sum to one and masked positions receive zero.

variants.title: Compute attention
variants.context: Scaled dot-product attention: project Q, K, V; take query-key dot products; divide by the square root of the key dimension; replace disallowed scores with a negative-infinite mask; normalize with softmax; take the weighted sum of values.
variants.prompt: Padding tokens must be ignored. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Weighted sum of values.
Score queries against keys.
Scale by √d_k.
Softmax over what remains.
Mask padding positions and any causally hidden positions.
Project Q, K, and V.

variants.hint: Padding masks and causal masks compose.
variants.explanation: All-masked rows must be rejected instead of producing undefined values.

variants.title: Compute attention
variants.context: Scaled dot-product attention: project Q, K, V; take query-key dot products; divide by the square root of the key dimension; replace disallowed scores with a negative-infinite mask; normalize with softmax; take the weighted sum of values.
variants.prompt: Why divide by √d_k? Put the steps in order, with the scaling step in place.

items.text: Compute dot products.
Apply the mask.
Blend values.
Normalize.
Project the vectors.
Scale so large key dimensions do not make softmax unnecessarily sharp.

variants.hint: Large dot products would saturate softmax without scaling.
variants.explanation: Scaling keeps the distribution trainable as dimensions grow.

variants.title: Size the KV cache
variants.context: KV bytes = 2 × layers × batch × cached tokens × KV heads × head dimension × bytes per element. Prefill builds the cache in parallel with quadratic query-key pairs; decode reads it one token at a time.
variants.prompt: 32 layers, batch 1, 1,024 cached tokens, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128, 2 bytes per element. How many MiB does the KV cache use?
variants.hint: 2 × layers × batch × tokens × KV heads × head dim × bytes.

mistakes.feedback: Keys and values both count: the leading factor is 2.
Two bytes per element, not four.

variants.hint: Scale the batch-1 result by eight.
variants.explanation: 128 MiB × 8 = 1,024 MiB, or 1 GiB, of cache before weights.

variants.prompt: A prompt has 2,000 tokens. With full attention, how many query-key pairs does prefill evaluate in one head of one layer?
variants.explanation: 2,000 × 2,000 = 4,000,000 pairs; the work grows quadratically with prompt length.

mistakes.feedback: Each query attends to every key.

variants.title: Separate the phases
variants.context: Prefill processes the prompt in parallel and pays quadratic pairwise work; decode emits one token at a time and reads the accumulated cache. IO-aware kernels avoid materializing the attention matrix but do not remove the pairwise work.
variants.prompt: A team doubles prompt length and sees prefill time far more than double. Why?
options: The tokenizer slowed down on the longer input string.
Decode ran twice, once per half of the longer prompt.
Query-key pairs grow quadratically with prompt length.
optionFeedback: Tokenization is linear in input length, so it cannot explain more than a doubling.
Decode cost is paid per output token and does not split by prompt halves.
variants.hint: How many pairs does a prompt of length n create?
variants.explanation: Prefill cost is quadratic in prompt length.

variants.title: Separate the phases
variants.context: Prefill processes the prompt in parallel and pays quadratic pairwise work; decode emits one token at a time and reads the accumulated cache. IO-aware kernels avoid materializing the attention matrix but do not remove the pairwise work.
variants.prompt: Does FlashAttention remove the quadratic attention work?
options: Yes; tiling reduces the pairwise comparisons to a linear scan.
Yes, for decode only, since decode reads the cache instead.
No. It avoids materializing the attention matrix in memory.
optionFeedback: Tiling changes how the matrix is read and written, and every query-key pair is still computed.
Decode reads the accumulated cache anyway, and the kernel does not change how many pairs exist.
IO-aware kernels save memory traffic, not the underlying computation.
variants.hint: Which resource does the kernel save?
variants.explanation: IO-aware kernels change memory behavior, not the attention contract.

variants.prompt: Which factors make the KV cache a serving constraint?
options: Only the parameter count, since the cache sits beside the weights.
Only the vocabulary size, which sets the width of each cached row.
Batch size, context length, KV heads, head dimension, layer count, and cache precision.
optionFeedback: Weights are separate from the cache, and they do not grow as a sequence gets longer.
Vocabulary size affects the output head, not the key and value tensors held per layer.
Every active sequence consumes cache that grows with context.
variants.hint: What does each active sequence hold in memory?
variants.explanation: Reconcile the planning estimate with runtime measurements.
